lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you met saving and investing. What is a dividend? (A share of a company's profit paid to its owners.) Today: shares, bonds and savings compared, spreading risk, and growing money over the long term.

Savings accounts are very safe and pay a little interest. Bonds lend money to a government or a company for set interest. Shares make you a part-owner of a company: they can grow a lot, or fall. Higher possible returns usually mean higher risk.

Risk means the value can go down as well as up. A single company can fail, and share prices rise and fall from day to day. Over many years, shares in many companies have usually grown faster than savings, with bumpy years on the way.

Don't put all your eggs in one basket: spread money across many companies, countries and kinds of investment. This is diversifying. A fund pools many people's money to buy hundreds of shares, so one company going bust hurts less.
Time helps, because growth earns more growth. The rule of 72 guesses how long money takes to double: 72 ÷ the yearly rate. At 6% a year, money doubles in about 12 years.

Inflation means prices rising. If savings earn 2% a year while prices rise 4%, your money buys less each year: the real return is 2 − 4, which is −2%. Investing aims to beat inflation over the long term.

Investing is not gambling: you own part of real businesses that make things and earn profits. Gambling and 'get rich quick' schemes are designed so most people lose. Beware anyone promising guaranteed high returns: it is often a scam.

Try it in the world: watch the money tree grow at the bank in My Money Stall, in Life. Then plant three small gardens in your village instead of one big one: if one fails, the others still grow. Next: consumer rights.

exercises.prompt: What do you own when you buy a share?
choices: a small part of a company
exercises.hint: Think of the word 'share': a part of something.
exercises.explain: A share is a small part of a company: you become a part-owner.

exercises.prompt: Savings accounts are usually lower risk than shares.
exercises.explain: True: savings are very safe; shares can rise or fall.

exercises.prompt: By the rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at 8% a year?

choices: put it all in one company
exercises.explain: Diversifying means spreading money across many investments, so one loss hurts less.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order of risk, lowest first.
exercises.hint: Look at the scatter graph from left to right.
exercises.explain: Savings, then a bond, then many shares, then one new company: risk rises.

exercises.prompt: Savings earn 2% a year while prices rise 5%. What is the real return, in percent? (It can be below 0.)
exercises.hint: Take the inflation rate from the interest rate.
exercises.explain: 2 − 5 gives −3%: the money buys less each year.

exercises.prompt: Match each investment to what it is.
exercises.hint: Owning, lending, pooling and keeping safe.
exercises.explain: A share: ownership. A bond: a loan. A fund: pooled money. Savings: a safe place for cash.

items: spinning a wheel for a prize
lending to a government in a bond
a fund that owns hundreds of firms
exercises.hint: Do you own part of something real, or is it chance designed so most people lose?
exercises.explain: Investing: shares, a fund, a bond. Gambling: betting, scratch cards, spinning wheels.

exercises.prompt: 1,000 gold grows at 6% a year. Using the rule of 72, about how much is it worth after 12 years?
exercises.hint: Find how long one doubling takes.
exercises.explain: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years: one doubling, so about 2,000 gold.

exercises.prompt: A promise of guaranteed high returns is often a scam.
exercises.explain: True: real investments can fall; anyone promising high returns with no risk is a warning sign.

exercises.prompt: Someone puts all their savings into one company, and it fails. What does this teach?
exercises.hint: Think of eggs and baskets again.
exercises.explain: Diversify: spread money across many investments, so one company going bust does not lose everything.

exercises.prompt: 3,000 gold is split equally between 3 companies. One fails and is worth 0; the other two each grow by 20%. What is the money worth now?
exercises.hint: Find each part, then grow the two that survive.

exercises.prompt: Why does time matter so much when investing?
choices: growth earns more growth over many years
exercises.hint: Think of the bars in the savings picture.
exercises.explain: Over many years growth adds to growth, and bumpy years even out.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: lower risk or higher risk?
exercises.hint: Could much of the money be lost?
exercises.explain: Lower: savings, a government bond, cash in a bank. Higher: one new company, get-rich-quick schemes, borrowing to bet.
False: share prices rise and fall, and a company can fail.
